q: Your P95 jumps noticeably every time you rerun with a new seed. What is most likely wrong?
o: too few runs for that tail: few runs lie beyond the P95
why: Tail percentiles need enough runs beyond them; plan N or use variance reduction.

q: Which method for estimating a 1-in-10,000 event within a few percent?
o: importance sampling (or very many plain runs)
why: Plain sampling needs about 100/p = 1 million runs for 10% error; importance sampling needs far fewer.

q: Plain sampling: how many runs for 10% relative error on p = 1/10,000?
why: About 100 hits needed: N ≈ 100/p = 1,000,000.

q: A bid's plan uses most likely inputs and shows profit 62,400; the simulation's mean is 39,400. The gap is mainly …
o: the flaw of averages: skew, a convex penalty and correlation
why: With MCSE around 100, the gap is model structure, not noise.

q: P(loss) = 0.182 with MCSE 0.0009. How many MCSEs above a 15% limit is it? (whole number)
why: (0.182 − 0.150)/0.0009 ≈ 36: no need for more runs.

q: If two scenarios differ by less than their MCSEs, the better-looking one should be chosen.
why: Myth. The difference is noise; use common random numbers or more runs to resolve it.

q: You compare order quantities 1,100 and 1,200. The sharpest comparison uses …
o: the same demand draws for both (common random numbers)
why: Shared draws make the noise cancel in the difference.

q: Price 25, cost 10, salvage 4. What is the newsvendor critical ratio (25 − 10)/(25 − 4)? (3 decimals)
why: 15/21 ≈ 0.714: order up to that demand quantile.

q: Ordering the average demand maximises expected profit for a seasonal product.
why: Myth. The best order is the demand quantile at the critical ratio, here about the 71st percentile.

q: Eight parallel workers give suspiciously smooth results and a tiny MCSE. First check?
o: whether workers share a seed (count distinct first draws)
why: Duplicated streams make runs repeat and the MCSE too small.

q: A pilot gives s = 400. Runs needed for a 95% half-width of 10? (nearest hundred)
MCSE of a mean with outcome SD 400,000 and 500 runs? (nearest thousand)
Durations are drawn from a normal and negative values are clipped to 0. The fix is …
o: use a positive distribution such as lognormal or gamma
why: A distribution with the right support avoids silent bias from clipping.

q: Labour and materials overruns share a cause. The model should …
o: link them with correlation or a common shock
why: Ignoring the common cause understates the tail of total cost.

q: A P50 cost is a sensible committed budget.
why: Myth. It is exceeded half the time; commit to a stated percentile such as P80 and show the range.

q: Your MCMC posterior mean has a naive s/√N error bar. What should you use instead?
o: an error bar based on effective sample size or batch means
why: Autocorrelated draws carry less information than their count suggests.

q: A risk model's 99.9th percentile is reported from 5,000 runs. The main problem?
o: it rests on about 5 runs beyond it
why: 0.1% of 5,000 is 5 runs: far too few to estimate that tail.

q: Before presenting, which check catches a logic bug fastest?
o: set inputs to fixed values with a known answer
why: A deterministic case with a known result isolates the logic from randomness.

q: You have 4 workers and spawn streams from SeedSequence(2026). How many numbers must you record to reproduce the whole run?
why: The parent seed reproduces every child stream.

q: A one-hour-per-run engineering model needs a tail probability. Best plan?
o: a fitted surrogate or a small designed experiment, with importance sampling where possible
a single run at average inputs
why: Expensive models need fewer, smarter runs; a single average-input run suffers the flaw of averages.

q: A small MCSE proves the model's inputs are right.
why: False. MCSE measures computing error only, not whether the inputs or structure are right.

q: FiveThirtyEight's 'wins in 71% of simulations' means …
o: the candidate gets 71% of the vote
the candidate won 71% of simulated elections
why: It is a win probability across simulated outcomes, not a vote share.
